name: scorecard
title: How Far Did We Get?
kicker: The measuring stick, applied · marks for discussion
html:
How Far Did We Get?

2000 · constraints

Met:

Not used: optional, and he says so.

2008 · rules

Met:

Partly: only HTTP so far.

The three R’s

Met: refused before sending, with a reason. replay with no model.

Partly: Buster’s pack written; not yet run against every client.

Further than most people expect, and not all the way yet.
say: So, how far did we get? Here's the measuring stick from the start, applied honestly. Fielding's 2000 constraints: client-server, stateless, cache, the uniform interface with hypermedia driving the state, and layering, with our gateway in front of GitHub, all met. Code on demand we didn't use; it's optional, and he says so. His 2008 rules: we enter by a bookmark, we don't fix URIs, the media type and the relation types carry the meaning, and HTTP is used as HTTP defines it, validators and all. Any protocol? Partly. We've only run over HTTP. Then the three R's. Right behavior: met; the second merge was refused before it left the machine, with the service's reason. Repeatability: met; the kept script replays with no model. Resilience: partly. Buster's pack is written and judging ARTIE, but I haven't run the whole pack against every client yet. That's the honest answer: further than most people expect, and not all the way yet.

sources.label: Fielding: REST APIs must be hypertext-driven (2008)

alternate.title: This slide as a plain page

deck:ref.name: client-server
deck:ref.label: CLIENT-SERVER
deck:ref.title: Client–server (§5.1.2)
deck:ref.summary: Separate the user interface from the data; let each side evolve on its own.
deck:ref.quote: “The first constraints added to our hybrid style are those of the client-server architectural style (Figure 5-2), described in Section 3.4.1. Separation of concerns is the principle behind the client-server constraints. By separating the user interface concerns from the data storage concerns, we improve the portability of the user interface across multiple platforms and improve scalability by simplifying the server components. Perhaps most significant to the Web, however, is that the separation allows the components to evolve independently, thus supporting the Internet-scale requirement of multiple organizational domains.”
deck:ref.cite: Roy T. Fielding, Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, §5.1.2

describedby.title: Roy T. Fielding, Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, §5.1.2

deck:ref.name: stateless
deck:ref.label: STATELESS
deck:ref.title: Stateless (§5.1.3)
deck:ref.summary: Every request carries all it needs; session state lives on the client.
deck:ref.quote: “We next add a constraint to the client-server interaction: communication must be stateless in nature, as in the client-stateless-server (CSS) style of Section 3.4.3 (Figure 5-3), such that each request from client to server must contain all of the information necessary to understand the request, and cannot take advantage of any stored context on the server. Session state is therefore kept entirely on the client.”
deck:ref.cite: Roy T. Fielding, Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, §5.1.3

describedby.title: Roy T. Fielding, Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, §5.1.3

deck:ref.name: cache
deck:ref.label: CACHE
deck:ref.title: Cache (§5.1.4)
deck:ref.summary: Label every response cacheable or not, so interactions can be skipped. HEART's L2 form sets are this.
deck:ref.quote:
“In order to improve network efficiency, we add cache constraints to form the client-cache-stateless-server style of Section 3.4.4 (Figure 5-4). Cache constraints require that the data within a response to a request be implicitly or explicitly labeled as cacheable or non-cacheable. If a response is cacheable, then a client cache is given the right to reuse that response data for later, equivalent requests.

The advantage of adding cache constraints is that they have the potential to partially or completely eliminate some interactions, improving efficiency, scalability, and user-perceived performance by reducing the average latency of a series of interactions. The trade-off, however, is that a cache can decrease reliability if stale data within the cache differs significantly from the data that would have been obtained had the request been sent directly to the server.”
deck:ref.cite: Roy T. Fielding, Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, §5.1.4

describedby.title: Roy T. Fielding, Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, §5.1.4

deck:ref.name: uniform-interface
deck:ref.label: UNIFORM-INTERFACE
deck:ref.title: Uniform interface (§5.1.5)
deck:ref.summary: One generic interface for every component; its fourth part is hypermedia as the engine of application state.
deck:ref.quote:
“The central feature that distinguishes the REST architectural style from other network-based styles is its emphasis on a uniform interface between components (Figure 5-6). By applying the software engineering principle of generality to the component interface, the overall system architecture is simplified and the visibility of interactions is improved. Implementations are decoupled from the services they provide, which encourages independent evolvability. The trade-off, though, is that a uniform interface degrades efficiency, since information is transferred in a standardized form rather than one which is specific to an application's needs. The REST interface is designed to be efficient for large-grain hypermedia data transfer, optimizing for the common case of the Web, but resulting in an interface that is not optimal for other forms of architectural interaction.

In order to obtain a uniform interface, multiple architectural constraints are needed to guide the behavior of components. REST is defined by four interface constraints: identification of resources; manipulation of resources through representations; self-descriptive messages; and, hypermedia as the engine of application state. These constraints will be discussed in Section 5.2.”
deck:ref.cite: Roy T. Fielding, Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, §5.1.5

describedby.title: Roy T. Fielding, Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, §5.1.5

deck:ref.name: layered-system
deck:ref.label: LAYERED
deck:ref.title: Layered system (§5.1.6)
deck:ref.summary: Each component sees only the next layer; intermediaries can cache and enforce policy. A gateway in front of GitHub is this.
deck:ref.quote: “In order to further improve behavior for Internet-scale requirements, we add layered system constraints (Figure 5-7). As described in Section 3.4.2, the layered system style allows an architecture to be composed of hierarchical layers by constraining component behavior such that each component cannot "see" beyond the immediate layer with which they are interacting. By restricting knowledge of the system to a single layer, we place a bound on the overall system complexity and promote substrate independence. Layers can be used to encapsulate legacy services and to protect new services from legacy clients, simplifying components by moving infrequently used functionality to a shared intermediary. Intermediaries can also be used to improve system scalability by enabling load balancing of services across multiple networks and processors.”
deck:ref.cite: Roy T. Fielding, Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, §5.1.6

describedby.title: Roy T. Fielding, Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, §5.1.6

deck:ref.name: code-on-demand
deck:ref.label: CODE-ON-DEMAND
deck:ref.title: Code-on-demand (§5.1.7)
deck:ref.summary: Clients may be extended by code the server sends; optional, because it reduces visibility.
deck:ref.quote: “The final addition to our constraint set for REST comes from the code-on-demand style of Section 3.5.3 (Figure 5-8). REST allows client functionality to be extended by downloading and executing code in the form of applets or scripts. This simplifies clients by reducing the number of features required to be pre-implemented. Allowing features to be downloaded after deployment improves system extensibility. However, it also reduces visibility, and thus is only an optional constraint within REST.”
deck:ref.cite: Roy T. Fielding, Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, §5.1.7

describedby.title: Roy T. Fielding, Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, §5.1.7

deck:ref.name: rule-2
deck:ref.label: PROTOCOL-AS-IS
deck:ref.title: Don't change the protocol
deck:ref.summary: In brief: fill in the protocol's underspecified bits; keep workarounds apart; interfaces stay generic.
deck:ref.quote: “A REST API should not contain any changes to the communication protocols aside from filling-out or fixing the details of underspecified bits of standard protocols, such as HTTP’s PATCH method or Link header field. Workarounds for broken implementations (such as those browsers stupid enough to believe that HTML defines HTTP’s method set) should be defined separately, or at least in appendices, with an expectation that the workaround will eventually be obsolete. [Failure here implies that the resource interfaces are object-specific, not generic.]”
deck:ref.cite: Roy T. Fielding, “REST APIs must be hypertext-driven”

describedby.title: Roy T. Fielding, “REST APIs must be hypertext-driven”

deck:ref.name: rule-3
deck:ref.label: MEDIA-TYPES
deck:ref.title: Spend the effort on media types
deck:ref.summary: In brief: describe media types and relations, not which methods go to which URIs. This is what HEART's spec is.
deck:ref.quote: “A REST API should spend almost all of its descriptive effort in defining the media type(s) used for representing resources and driving application state, or in defining extended relation names and/or hypertext-enabled mark-up for existing standard media types. Any effort spent describing what methods to use on what URIs of interest should be entirely defined within the scope of the processing rules for a media type (and, in most cases, already defined by existing media types). [Failure here implies that out-of-band information is driving interaction instead of hypertext.]”
deck:ref.cite: Roy T. Fielding, “REST APIs must be hypertext-driven”

describedby.title: Roy T. Fielding, “REST APIs must be hypertext-driven”

deck:ref.name: rule-4
deck:ref.label: NO-FIXED-URIS
deck:ref.title: No fixed resource names or hierarchies
deck:ref.summary: In brief: the server owns its namespace and tells the client how to build addresses: forms, URI templates.
deck:ref.quote: “A REST API must not define fixed resource names or hierarchies (an obvious coupling of client and server). Servers must have the freedom to control their own namespace. Instead, allow servers to instruct clients on how to construct appropriate URIs, such as is done in HTML forms and URI templates, by defining those instructions within media types and link relations. [Failure here implies that clients are assuming a resource structure due to out-of band information, such as a domain-specific standard, which is the data-oriented equivalent to RPC’s functional coupling].”
deck:ref.cite: Roy T. Fielding, “REST APIs must be hypertext-driven”

describedby.title: Roy T. Fielding, “REST APIs must be hypertext-driven”

deck:ref.name: rule-5
deck:ref.label: NO-TYPES
deck:ref.title: No resource types the client depends on
deck:ref.summary: In brief: the client knows media types and relation names, nothing about what kind of thing is behind them.
deck:ref.quote: “A REST API should never have “typed” resources that are significant to the client. Specification authors may use resource types for describing server implementation behind the interface, but those types must be irrelevant and invisible to the client. The only types that are significant to a client are the current representation’s media type and standardized relation names. [ditto]”
deck:ref.cite: Roy T. Fielding, “REST APIs must be hypertext-driven”

describedby.title: Roy T. Fielding, “REST APIs must be hypertext-driven”

deck:ref.name: rule-6
deck:ref.label: BOOKMARK
deck:ref.title: Enter with a bookmark; follow what's offered
deck:ref.summary: In brief: one URI and known media types to start; every next step chosen from what the server put in the answer.
deck:ref.quote: “A REST API should be entered with no prior knowledge beyond the initial URI (bookmark) and set of standardized media types that are appropriate for the intended audience (i.e., expected to be understood by any client that might use the API). From that point on, all application state transitions must be driven by client selection of server-provided choices that are present in the received representations or implied by the user’s manipulation of those representations. The transitions may be determined (or limited by) the client’s knowledge of media types and resource communication mechanisms, both of which may be improved on-the-fly (e.g., code-on-demand). [Failure here implies that out-of-band information is driving interaction instead of hypertext.]”
deck:ref.cite: Roy T. Fielding, “REST APIs must be hypertext-driven”

describedby.title: Roy T. Fielding, “REST APIs must be hypertext-driven”

deck:ref.name: rule-1
deck:ref.label: ANY-PROTOCOL
deck:ref.title: Not tied to one communication protocol
deck:ref.summary: In brief: identification is separate from interaction; any URI scheme may identify.
deck:ref.quote: “A REST API should not be dependent on any single communication protocol, though its successful mapping to a given protocol may be dependent on the availability of metadata, choice of methods, etc. In general, any protocol element that uses a URI for identification must allow any URI scheme to be used for the sake of that identification. [Failure here implies that identification is not separated from interaction.]”
deck:ref.cite: Roy T. Fielding, “REST APIs must be hypertext-driven”

describedby.title: Roy T. Fielding, “REST APIs must be hypertext-driven”

deck:ref.name: right-behavior
deck:ref.label: RIGHT-BEHAVIOR
deck:ref.title: Right behavior: only what the state allows, and a reason when not
deck:ref.summary: The agent is offered only the acts the current state allows, sends each one with the validator from the state it read, and gets a reason when an act is absent. At the small scale it is a Gherkin scenario that says what right means before any code is written.
deck:ref.cite: The first of the three R's

describedby.title: The first of the three R's

deck:ref.name: repeatability
deck:ref.label: REPEATABILITY
deck:ref.title: Repeatability: the same goal, the same result, every time
deck:ref.summary: Reliability and repeatability are the same thing here. Found once with a model, then replayed with none: the same steps, the same checks, the same result, until the controls really change. At the small scale it is one scenario that runs the same way every time.
deck:ref.cite: The second of the three R's

describedby.title: The second of the three R's

deck:ref.name: resilience
deck:ref.label: RESILIENCE
deck:ref.title: Resilience: the server changes, the client doesn't break
deck:ref.summary: When the server changes, or misbehaves on purpose, the client takes the failure path the spec names, re-syncs, and goes on; a model comes back only when the controls really changed, to repair. At the small scale it is the regression suite and the gates that hold, even against the model.
deck:ref.cite: The third of the three R's

describedby.title: The third of the three R's
